attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post. Nothing in the sentence is quoted from someone else except the scare-quoted phrase about demand.

semantics.note: The revision keeps the 3GW figure as an assumption, keeps 'theoretically' and keeps 'appears to be showing'. It is a present-state observation about reported revenue, not a forecast.

contract.note: Reading 2025 as the period and 'tens of billions' as roughly $20B or more is an ordinary plain reading. Requiring revenue tied to the same new US capacity is demanding but matches what he asserted. The ambiguity flags are acknowledged.

evidence.note: CoreWeave's own earnings remarks give more than $5.1B of consolidated 2025 revenue. They do not separate new US capacity from older or non-US facilities, so they cannot confirm or refute the cohort shortfall.

reviews.rationale: The packet does not identify the assumed 3GW cohort, does not tie any revenue to it, and does not test the theoretical revenue calculation. The only item is consolidated revenue for one operator, which is context. The evidence does not settle either the expectation or the claimed shortfall.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence, his own conclusion after summarizing the Kedrosky/Wood Mackenzie figures.

semantics.note: In context, 'they' is the roughly 61GW IT-load cohort in active development. The hypothetical 'even if they were' is kept. This is a present-state claim about power availability.

contract.note: Judging whether there is enough deliverable power for the whole cohort, at a Q4 2025 baseline, is an ordinary reading. It neither turns the claim into a never-available forecast nor counts national nameplate capacity as enough.

evidence.note: Wood Mackenzie reports that PJM large-load commitments are about three times its risked generation queue. This is regional and not matched to project sites, so it does not account for power across the 61GW cohort.
PJM's own shortfall paper is about the 2027/28 capacity auction in a single region. It shows constraints but does not measure present deliverable power for the nationwide cohort.

reviews.rationale: Both items show regional power stress, mainly in PJM. Neither gives the site-matched accounting of grid and on-site power for the cohort that the contract requires. The packet is consistent with the claim but does not establish it or refute it.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words: an inference he draws from his premise about LLMs writing all code.

semantics.note: The normalised text drops 'or solve software architecture issues', which is part of what he asserted; the contract keeps it. 'LLM mandates push' is a fair gloss of 'incentivized' in context. The 'almost every major tech company' scope is kept.

contract.note: Requiring near-universal coverage for 'almost every', and separating adoption mandates from incentives against learning, is an ordinary reading of firm language. The contract includes both coding and architecture.

evidence.note: Reporting before the post on Meta tying reviews to AI use. Meta says it assesses impact, not usage. One company, and nothing showing rewards for abandoning learning.
Anthropic's trial (a company disclosure) found lower short-term mastery with AI help, but the result depended on how AI was used. It tests a mechanism, not employer incentives or how common they are.

reviews.rationale: The packet has a report about one employer and a short lab study of a mechanism. There is no policy inventory across major tech companies and no workplace evidence linking incentives to stopped learning or to architecture skills. That is not enough to support or contradict the broad causal claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence. 'They' refers back to companies that incentivize token burn.

semantics.note: Captures the core assertion: rewarding token use guarantees poor software. The motive clause ('because everybody else is') is left out, which is acceptable because it is a separate side assertion. The wording is hyperbolic but it is a firm causal claim.

contract.note: Reading 'guaranteeing' as necessary causation, so that one good counterexample would refute it, is the ordinary reading of his word. The contract correctly separates token-reward policies from ordinary AI adoption.

evidence.note: Google DORA commentary reports verification and review costs from AI coding. It does not examine token-consumption rewards or measure maintenance outcomes, so it neither establishes the guarantee nor provides a counterexample.

reviews.rationale: No item documents a token-reward policy together with measured software quality. DORA shows general AI tradeoffs only. The packet establishes neither a necessary causal link nor a verified counterexample, so the claim cannot be scored.
